summary: This bash script defines three assertion functions for validation: one checks if a variable is empty and optionally prints an error, another verifies a command-line binary exists on the system, and the third checks whether a Docker image is available locally. These are utility functions that help scripts fail fast with clear error messages when prerequisites aren't met.

explanations.4: The ${1:-} syntax grabs the first argument passed to the function, or defaults to an empty string if no argument was provided. The -r flag makes it read-only so it can't be accidentally modified.
explanations.7: [[ -z ${variable} ]] checks if the variable is empty (zero length). The && operator means 'if true, then do the next thing', so this line only prints the error message if the variable is actually empty.
explanations.18: command -v checks if a binary exists in your PATH. The || true at the end prevents the function from crashing if the command isn't found—we want to capture the result regardless.
explanations.29: This uses parameter expansion to embed the imageName variable directly into the string. When you double-quote a string with $ inside, bash substitutes the variable's value.
explanations.34: docker images -q returns just the image ID if the image exists, or nothing if it doesn't. The 2> /dev/null silently discards any error messages from docker. If the result equals an empty string, the image doesn't exist.
